lessonTitle: Portfolios, Reflection and Career Planning: Learning from Practice in the UK Foundation Years

blocks.text: In the middle of your first night on call you catch a blood sample that is about to be sent with another patient's label on it. You relabel it correctly and nothing bad happens. A week later your supervisor asks, 'What have you learned from your first month?' and you cannot remember a single specific example. Doctors learn constantly but forget unless they record and reflect, which is the purpose of the portfolio.

blocks.markdown: Medicine is a career-long learning profession. In the UK, learning is documented in a **portfolio** (an e-portfolio in the Foundation Programme), reviewed with supervisors, and continued through appraisal and **revalidation** for life. This unit covers how to keep a reflective portfolio and extract learning points, the main stages of postgraduate training and licensing in outline, and how to build a personal development plan and use mentors. Systems, platforms and requirements change, so always check the current Foundation Programme, General Medical Council (GMC) and local guidance.

blocks.title: Reflective practice
blocks.text: The habit of thinking systematically about an experience (what happened, how you thought and felt, what it meant and what you will do differently) so that experience becomes learning. Reflection is not just description and is not self-criticism; it ends in a concrete change in knowledge, skill or behaviour.

blocks.markdown: A structured model keeps reflection from becoming a diary entry. A common model is **Gibbs' reflective cycle**: description, feelings, evaluation, analysis, conclusion and action plan. Others include Kolb's cycle of experience, reflection, conceptualisation and experimentation. The best reflections are short, specific and honest, include what you would do differently and, importantly, show follow-through when you revisit the action. Reflection should be anonymised: remove patient names, hospital numbers, dates of birth and anything that could identify patients or colleagues, in line with GMC and Academy of Medical Royal Colleges guidance on reflective practice, which you should check in its current form.

rows: Give the facts briefly: setting, task, outcome
What were you thinking and feeling?
What was good and bad about it?
Both your actions and the system
Why did it happen and what does evidence or guidance say?
Link to guidelines, theory or colleague advice
What did you learn, and what else could you have done?
What will you do next time, and by when?
blocks.caption: Gibbs' reflective cycle as a structure for portfolio entries.

blocks.title: Writing a reflective entry from a near miss
blocks.prompt: On a night shift you noticed that a blood sample for a crossmatch was labelled with another patient's details. You stopped, checked the wristband against the request form, relabelled it and reported the near miss. Write a short reflective entry using Gibbs' cycle.

steps.text: Description: 'During a night shift I found a blood sample labelled with the details of a different patient. I stopped, checked the identity band at the bedside, relabelled the sample and told the nurse in charge.' No patient identifiers are included.

Feelings and evaluation: 'I felt alarmed and slightly embarrassed, then relieved that I had checked. What went well was that I paused and verified identity. What went badly was that I had labelled samples away from the bedside while rushing.'

Analysis: 'Labelling away from the patient is a recognised cause of wrong-blood-in-tube errors, which can lead to harmful transfusions. Local policy requires identity checks at the bedside.' Link to the trust policy and, where appropriate, current national guidance.
Conclusion: 'I learned that time pressure increases the risk of identification errors and that near misses are valuable for learning.'

Action plan: 'From now on I will label samples at the bedside after checking the wristband, and I will discuss my learning at my next supervisor meeting within two weeks.' Record the incident report as a separate step in the incident system.

blocks.answer: A good entry is anonymised, honest, linked to evidence or policy and ends in a specific, dated action; the near miss is also reported through the incident system.

blocks.markdown: **What a portfolio contains.** The Foundation Programme e-portfolio records evidence of progress: supervised learning events (such as direct observation of procedures or case-based discussions), team assessments of behaviour, reflections, teaching delivered, quality improvement or audit activity, attendance at required teaching, and supervisor meetings and reports. Exact requirements are set by the UK Foundation Programme and your foundation school, so check the current curriculum. The aim is to show reflective learning, not to collect forms. Review and sign-off by your educational supervisor and an annual review of progress are required to move on.

**Training and licensing in outline (UK).** After graduation from medical school, doctors usually begin the two-year Foundation Programme. UK graduates receive provisional GMC registration with a licence to practise for the first foundation year (FY1); after satisfactory completion of FY1 they can apply for full registration. Following the second foundation year (FY2), doctors enter specialty training, for example core or internal medicine training, general practice training or run-through programmes, followed by higher specialty training in a chosen specialty. On completion of an approved programme, they receive a **Certificate of Completion of Training (CCT)** and are eligible for the GMC's specialist or GP register and consultant or GP posts. Other routes exist, and durations vary by specialty, so check the current curricula of the relevant Royal College. Throughout practice, a doctor must hold a licence to practise and **revalidate**, usually every five years, on the basis of annual appraisal, reflection on feedback and evidence of continuing professional development.

First year of the Foundation Programme

Full registration after FY1; broader responsibility and further portfolio evidence
Core, internal medicine, GP or run-through programmes

blocks.title: Registration, licence and revalidation are different things
blocks.text: Registration puts you on the medical register; a licence to practise allows you to carry out regulated activities; revalidation is the periodic process by which a licensed doctor shows they remain fit to practise, through appraisal, feedback and learning. Reflection in your portfolio is one of the inputs to the process.

blocks.markdown: **Personal development plans and mentors.** A personal development plan (PDP) turns identified learning needs into actions. Find needs from feedback, supervised learning events, incidents and your curriculum. State each objective in a **SMART** form: specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound. Decide the resources and who will help, set a review date, and update the plan after each review. A **mentor** is a more experienced colleague who offers confidential, developmental and voluntary support, such as career advice and perspective; this differs from your **educational supervisor**, who is assigned, assesses your progress and writes formal reports. A coach helps you reach your own goals through questioning. Choose a mentor whose experience you respect and with whom you can be honest, and agree how often to meet and what is confidential.

blocks.title: Writing a SMART learning objective
blocks.prompt: In your first rotation you realise that you are uncertain when interpreting electrocardiograms (ECGs) and a senior has suggested you improve. Turn this learning need into a SMART objective within a PDP and identify support.

steps.text: Define the need: use feedback and a reflective entry to state the gap: 'I lack confidence in systematically interpreting 12-lead ECGs and in knowing when to escalate.'
Write a specific, measurable objective: 'I will report and discuss 15 ECGs with a senior colleague, using a systematic approach, and record the learning points for each.'

Make it time-bound and achievable: 'I will complete this over the next 10 weeks, around 1 or 2 ECGs per week, using routine ward work and teaching sessions.' Check relevance to the foundation curriculum.

Identify resources and people: the cardiology teaching programme, a recommended textbook or e-learning module, a named senior or the specialist nurse, and your educational supervisor to review progress.
Set review and evidence: review at the mid-rotation meeting, record ECG discussions as supervised learning events or reflections in the portfolio, and decide a new objective if it is achieved.

blocks.answer: A SMART objective is specific (15 ECGs discussed with a senior), measurable, time-bound (10 weeks), relevant to the curriculum and supported by named people and review points.

blocks.title: Reflections are not a place to blame or identify
blocks.text: Never record identifiable patient details or personal criticism of colleagues in a portfolio. Serious incidents must be reported through the incident system, not only written about in the portfolio; reflection supplements formal reporting. Follow current GMC and Academy guidance about how reflective notes are used and how to protect them.

points: Reflection follows a structure such as Gibbs' cycle and ends with a specific action; keep entries anonymised and honest.

UK graduates have provisional registration in FY1, then full registration, foundation year 2, specialty training and a CCT before the specialist or GP register; revalidation continues throughout a licensed career.
A SMART personal development plan converts learning needs into actions with dates, resources and review points.
Mentors provide confidential, developmental support, whereas educational supervisors are assigned and assess progress.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best example of a reflective portfolio entry?

options.text: It blames a colleague for what went wrong
It records every detail of the event but draws no conclusion
It briefly describes an event, explores thoughts and feelings, analyses what happened using guidance or feedback, and ends with a specific action
It lists the patient's name and hospital number so the case can be traced

questions.correctOptionText: It briefly describes an event, explores thoughts and feelings, analyses what happened using guidance or feedback, and ends with a specific action

distractorRationale.a: Reflection focuses on learning, not blame.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: reflection moves from description to a planned change.

questions.explanation: Reflection involves analysis and planning, not only description, and should identify what you will do differently. Confidentiality and a non-blaming approach are essential.

questions.stem: Before uploading a reflection about a clinical event to your e-portfolio, what must you do?

options.text: Write only the colleague's name and omit what happened
Remove or anonymise patient and colleague identifiers such as names, hospital numbers and dates of birth
Include the hospital number so the supervisor can check the notes
Add the patient's full name for accuracy

questions.correctOptionText: Remove or anonymise patient and colleague identifiers such as names, hospital numbers and dates of birth

distractorRationale.a: Does not meet the purpose of reflection and still identifies a colleague.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: confidentiality applies to portfolio entries.
distractorRationale.c: Identifiable data should not be stored in the portfolio.

questions.explanation: Portfolio entries should not contain information that could identify patients or colleagues, in line with professional guidance on confidentiality. Reflection remains useful when the facts are described in general terms.

questions.stem: A UK medical graduate completes the first foundation year (FY1) satisfactorily. What is the usual next step in registration?

options.text: Application for full GMC registration, after which they continue in FY2
They automatically receive a Certificate of Completion of Training
They remain on provisional registration indefinitely
They revalidate immediately and leave the register

questions.correctOptionText: Application for full GMC registration, after which they continue in FY2

distractorRationale.a: Correct: full registration follows successful FY1.
distractorRationale.b: The CCT follows completion of specialty training.
distractorRationale.d: Revalidation is a periodic process for licensed doctors.

questions.explanation: UK graduates normally hold provisional registration with a licence during FY1 and then apply for full registration. A CCT comes at the end of specialty training, and revalidation is a later, periodic process; check the current GMC rules.

questions.stem: Revalidation of licensed doctors in the UK is usually repeated every five years and is supported by annual appraisal and evidence such as feedback and continuing professional development.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Revalidation is the GMC process by which licensed doctors show they remain fit to practise, normally on a five-year cycle informed by annual appraisal. Reflection on feedback and learning forms part of the evidence; check the latest rules.

questions.stem: A doctor finishes an approved specialty training programme. What does this normally lead to?

options.text: Provisional registration with a licence to practise
Automatic appointment as medical director
A Certificate of Completion of Training and eligibility for the GMC specialist or GP register
Annual review of the portfolio only

questions.correctOptionText: A Certificate of Completion of Training and eligibility for the GMC specialist or GP register

distractorRationale.a: This is the status at the start of FY1.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: the CCT marks completion of approved training.
distractorRationale.d: An annual review continues but is not the outcome of training.

questions.explanation: A CCT is awarded on completion of an approved training programme and allows entry to the specialist or GP register and consultant or GP posts. Details vary by pathway, so confirm the current rules.

questions.stem: Which learning objective is best written in SMART form?

options.text: Become an expert in medicine
Perform and be observed doing 10 supervised venepunctures with feedback from a senior over the next 8 weeks
Learn something about procedures sometime this year
Get better at practical skills

questions.correctOptionText: Perform and be observed doing 10 supervised venepunctures with feedback from a senior over the next 8 weeks
questions.explanation: SMART means specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound. The correct objective has a defined number, a clear method of observation and a deadline, while the others cannot be assessed.

questions.stem: Which description best separates a mentor from an educational supervisor?

options.text: A mentor offers confidential, developmental support and does not formally assess, whereas an educational supervisor is assigned and writes formal progress reports
A mentor signs off the annual review while the supervisor gives career advice
A mentor is always a more senior person from another country
They are the same role with different names

questions.correctOptionText: A mentor offers confidential, developmental support and does not formally assess, whereas an educational supervisor is assigned and writes formal progress reports

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the roles differ in purpose and assessment.

questions.explanation: Mentoring is usually voluntary and confidential, focusing on development and perspective. Educational supervisors have a formal role in assessing progress and reporting to the programme.

questions.stem: The morning after a busy on-call you realise that you did not review a chest radiograph you requested the previous evening. The report shows a new small pleural effusion that the registrar had already seen and acted on, and no harm occurred. Write the structure of a reflective entry using Gibbs' cycle, and say how it should be recorded and handled.
markingGuide: Description: brief, factual, anonymised account of the event
Feelings: honest account of thoughts and emotions
Evaluation: what went well (registrar reviewed the result, no harm) and what did not (result not reviewed by the requester)
Analysis: causes such as workload, lack of task list or handover for results, and links to guidance on test-result follow-up
Conclusion: learning points about owning results and using a checklist
Action plan: specific, dated change such as adding pending results to the handover list and reviewing at the next supervisor meeting
No patient or colleague identifiers; consider reporting the event through the incident system and discussing with the supervisor
questions.explanation: The entry should flow through the six stages and end in a concrete action. The event should also be reported through the incident system if local policy requires, because reflection supplements rather than replaces formal reporting.

questions.stem: You are in FY1 and unsure whether you want a career in general practice or in a hospital specialty. Describe how you would use a personal development plan and mentors to explore this, and outline the stages of training and licensing that follow FY1.
markingGuide: Identifies learning needs and interests through feedback, supervised learning events and reflection
Writes SMART objectives, for example taster experiences or audit, with dates and review
Uses the educational supervisor and chooses a mentor for confidential career advice
Seeks specialty-specific experience, teaching, audit or quality improvement and records it in the portfolio
Outlines FY1 provisional registration then full registration, FY2, specialty or GP training, CCT and entry to the specialist or GP register
Mentions revalidation with annual appraisal throughout practice
Notes that requirements vary and should be checked with current Foundation Programme, GMC and Royal College guidance
questions.explanation: A good plan converts uncertainty into specific, time-bound exploration and uses both a supervisor and a mentor. The pathway should be described accurately in outline with appropriate caveats about changing rules.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the proper use of a reflective portfolio after a serious incident on the ward?

options.text: Include full patient identifiers so the case can be reviewed
Report the incident through the formal system and use the portfolio to record honest, anonymised reflection and learning
Avoid reflecting on errors in case they are discovered
Write about the incident in the portfolio instead of reporting it

questions.correctOptionText: Report the incident through the formal system and use the portfolio to record honest, anonymised reflection and learning

distractorRationale.c: Honest reflection is part of learning; check current guidance on its use.
distractorRationale.d: Formal reporting is a separate professional duty.

questions.explanation: Incident reporting and reflection serve different purposes: reporting allows the organisation to investigate and fix system causes, while reflection builds personal learning. The entry must remain anonymised and honest, and you should follow current GMC and Academy guidance.
